item.title: Ames Housing - Part 2 - Building Models
item.description:
In a previous post in this series, we explored the Ames Housing dataset.

In this post, we build linear and non-linear models, and we find out how well they predict the SalePrice of properties. A model is a formula that a computer learns from examples. A linear model adds up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that it learns from the data. A non-linear model can also learn curved relationships.

Evaluation Criteria

To measure how good a model is, we use the root mean squared error (RMSE) between the log of the predicted price and the log of the actual SalePrice. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, so a lower RMSE is better. We use the log of the prices so that an error of 10% counts the same for an expensive house and for a cheap house.

Steps for Building Models

Each model has settings that it cannot learn from the data. We must choose them before training. These settings are called hyperparameters. To choose the best hyperparameters, we use K-fold cross validation, as described in the steps below:

  • Remove features that repeat the information of other features, and change ordinal features into scores.
  • Split the training data into K parts (folds). Each time, the model learns from all the folds except one (the training part), and we check its predictions on the remaining fold (the validation part). We split the data in a way that keeps a similar mix of prices in each fold (stratified sampling).
  • Choose the linear and non-linear models to use.
  • For each model, make a set (a grid) of hyperparameter combinations that covers the possible values evenly (a space-filling grid).
  • For each combination, train the model on the training part and make predictions on the validation part. Repeat this for all the folds.
  • Calculate the RMSE, and choose the combination with the lowest RMSE.
  • Train each model again, with its best combination, on the complete training set.
  • Calculate the RMSE of each final model on the testing set, which has properties that the models have not seen.
  • Choose the model with the lowest RMSE.

Removing Collinear Predictors

Many features in this dataset describe the same thing in different ways. Also, some of the features that we created in the previous post repeat others. A model cannot use categories directly, so each category becomes a separate feature with the values 0 and 1 (a dummy variable). After this change, some features are exact combinations of other features (we call them collinear). A linear model cannot separate the effects of collinear features. So its coefficients become unreliable, or it cannot calculate them at all, and lm (the basic linear model in R) gives a warning about a “rank-deficient fit”. Models that use decision trees are not affected by repeated information. But if we remove it, the linear models work correctly and all the models are simpler.

The association matrix in the previous post showed which features repeat each other. We drop these features, because other features already give their information:

  • HasGarage, HasFireplace and HasMasVnr are the same as, or almost the same as, the None category of GarageType, FireplaceQu and MasVnrType.
  • MSSubClass combines the type and the style of a building. BldgType and HouseStyle already give this information. Its duplex category is identical to the duplex category of BldgType.
  • TotalBath is exactly FullBath + 0.5 * HalfBath + BsmtBath. We drop HalfBath, not TotalBath. So we keep the total, which is one of the most important features for the decision tree models. And we lose no information, because we can calculate HalfBath from the other three features.

Encoding Ordinal Features

The categories of features such as OverallQual or KitchenQual have a natural order. These are ordinal features. By default, step_dummy() changes an ordinal feature into several features called polynomial contrasts. It makes one new feature for each category except one, and these features describe straight, curved and more complex trends across the grades. But some grades are very rare. For example, only one property has an OverallCond of 1. So a rare grade can be missing from a fold. Then some of these new features become collinear in that fold.

Instead, we change each ordinal feature into one whole number (a score) that follows the order of its categories: 1, 2, 3 and so on. This assumes that the steps between the grades are equal. First, we drop the categories that no property has, such as a Poor exterior quality, so that the scores have no gaps. Here are the results of a linear model with each method, on the same folds:

dfEncodingComparison %>% 
  mutate(lm_cv_rmse = round(lm_cv_rmse, 4)) %>% 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Encoding of ordinal features", "Predictors", "Folds with a rank-deficient fit", "lm cross validated RMSE"))
Encoding of ordinal features Predictors Folds with a rank-deficient fit lm cross validated RMSE
polynomial contrasts 214 4 0.1470
ordinal scores 151 0 0.1336 
encoding_value <- function(encodingName, column) dfEncodingComparison[[column]][dfEncodingComparison$encoding == encodingName]
  • With polynomial contrasts, lm cannot calculate all the coefficients in 4 of the 5 folds. With scores, this problem happens in 0 folds.
  • With scores, the number of features goes down from 214 to 151, and the cross validated RMSE of lm goes down from 0.147 to 0.134. The simpler method works better on new data, because the model does not have to learn a separate effect for each rare grade.

Finally, step_lincomb() checks whether any features are still exact combinations of other features. This could happen because properties without a basement or a garage have the None category in every basement or garage feature. With scores, it finds no such features.

After these steps, there are 151 features, and a linear model can calculate a coefficient for each of them:

model_lm_check <- lm(target ~ ., data = dfTrain_Proc %>% select(-Id))
print(glue::glue("{sum(is.na(coef(model_lm_check)))} of {length(coef(model_lm_check))} coefficients could not be estimated"))
0 of 152 coefficients could not be estimated

Partitioning Training Data

We split the training data into 5 folds. In each fold, the model learns from 80% of the data, and we compare its predictions with the actual prices on the other 20%.

Let’s look at the spread (distribution) of the target, which is the value that we want to predict, in all the folds:

cv_folds %>% 
  mutate(target = map(splits, function(Z) bind_rows(training(Z) %>% select(target) %>% mutate(type = "training"), 
                                                    testing(Z) %>% select(target) %>% mutate(type = "validation")))) %>% 
  select(-splits) %>% 
  unnest(cols = c(target)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = target)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "white", fill = "#F37735") +
  labs(x = "log(SalePrice)") +
  facet_grid(type ~ id)

Because we use stratified sampling, the prices have similar distributions in the training part and in the validation part of each fold.

Linear Models

Ordinary Least Squares Regression

First, we use cross validation to test a simple linear model on the training data. This model, called ordinary least squares, finds the straight-line formula with the smallest squared errors. Its result is our starting point (benchmark). If more complex models are not much better than this result, they are not worth the extra effort.

model_spec_lm
Linear Regression Model Specification (regression)

Computational engine: lm 
cv_results_lm
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_rmse
      <dbl>
1     0.134
rmse_val <- cv_results_lm %>% pull(mean_rmse)

What’s notable?

  • A linear model with all the features gives an RMSE of 0.1336.
  • This is the simplest and fastest model, and it has no hyperparameters to choose.

A residual is the difference between the actual value and the predicted value, here of log(SalePrice). Residual plots show if the errors of a model have a pattern. If the model is good, the residuals look like random noise around 0. Here are the four standard residual plots of the linear model, fitted on the complete training set. The labels show the Id of the most extreme properties in each plot:

eda_plot_residuals(model_lm_check, vLabels = dfTrain_Proc$Id, plotTitle = "Residual plots of the linear model")

# standardized residual, leverage and Cook's distance of each property
dfLmDiagnostics <- tibble(Id = dfTrain_Proc$Id,
                          std_resid = rstandard(model_lm_check),
                          leverage = hatvalues(model_lm_check),
                          cooks = cooks.distance(model_lm_check)) %>%
  arrange(desc(cooks))
lm_diagnostic <- function(propertyId, column) dfLmDiagnostics[[column]][dfLmDiagnostics$Id == propertyId]
  • Residuals vs Fitted: Most residuals are close to 0. But three properties have very large negative residuals: the model predicts much higher prices than their actual prices. These are Ids 1299, 524 and 633. In the previous post, we saw that 1299 and 524 are very large properties that sold at low prices.
  • Normal Q-Q: The lower tail is much longer than the dashed line. Property 1299 has a standardized residual of -12.4, and property 524 has -9.1. For normally distributed errors, values beyond -3 are very rare.
  • Scale-Location: The smooth line goes up at both ends, so the errors are larger for the cheapest and the most expensive properties.
  • Residuals vs Leverage: Properties 1299 and 524 have both a large residual and a high leverage (0.22 and 0.16). So they have the largest Cook’s distances, 0.29 and 0.11. These are below the dashed contour at 0.5, but much larger than for most properties. They pull the straight-line fit, which is one reason why glmnet and the tree-based models work better.

Regularized Linear Model

Next, we use glmnet, a linear model with regularization. Regularization adds a penalty for large coefficients. This makes the model keep only the effects that the data clearly supports. glmnet combines two types of regularization: LASSO (L1), which can reduce the coefficient of a feature to exactly 0, and Ridge (L2), which makes all the coefficients smaller. We search for the values of these hyperparameters that give the lowest RMSE:

  • penalty: the total amount of regularization in the model.
  • mixture: the share of LASSO (L1) regularization in the model.
model_spec_glmnet
Linear Regression Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  penalty = tune()
  mixture = tune()

Computational engine: glmnet

Here are the 10 best RMSE values and their hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_glmnet %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 3
    penalty mixture mean_rmse
      <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 1.46e- 2  0.297      0.129
 2 1.22e- 3  0.490      0.130
 3 1.09e- 2  0.0439     0.131
 4 3.47e- 4  0.992      0.131
 5 1.22e- 2  0.657      0.131
 6 8.18e- 4  0.0856     0.132
 7 7.37e- 7  0.0221     0.132
 8 1.15e- 4  0.798      0.132
 9 3.37e-10  0.0573     0.133
10 1.57e- 5  0.0760     0.133

What’s notable?

  • After we choose the hyperparameters with cross validation, the best glmnet model has an RMSE of 0.129, with penalty = 0.0146 and mixture = 0.2974.
  • This is better than the ordinary least squares model, which had an RMSE of 0.1336. The regularization makes the coefficients of the less useful features smaller. This helps when there are so many features.
  • Cross validation of glmnet is fast. It takes about 11 seconds.
  • But outliers can strongly affect its results.

Here is a plot of the glmnet hyperparameter grid, with the best combination:

eda_plot_scatter(param_grid_glmnet, "mixture", "penalty", alpha = 1, add_lm = F, yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::scientific) +
  geom_point(data = param_best_glmnet, aes(x = mixture, y = penalty), color = "red") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = param_best_glmnet %>% map_df(round, digits = 4), 
                            aes(x = mixture, y = penalty, label = glue::glue("penalty: {penalty}, mixture:{mixture}")),
                            family = "Roboto Condensed")

Non-linear Models

Next, we train two types of models that use decision trees. A decision tree predicts a value by asking a series of yes/no questions about the features, such as “Is TotalSF more than 2000?”. These models are not very sensitive to outliers and skewed data.

ranger (Random Forest)

A random forest builds many decision trees, each from a random sample of the data, and takes the average of their predictions. We use ranger, a version of random forests that gives the same results as the randomForest package but runs about 3 times faster. Each forest has 500 trees. (On a dataset of this size, more trees do not improve the error.) We search for the best values of these hyperparameters:

  • mtry: the number of features that the tree chooses from at random at each question (split).
  • min_n: the minimum number of properties that a group (node) must have before the tree can split it again.
model_spec_rf
Random Forest Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  mtry = tune()
  trees = 500
  min_n = tune()

Engine-Specific Arguments:
  num.threads = 1

Computational engine: ranger

Here are the 10 best RMSE values and their hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_rf %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 3
   min_n  mtry mean_rmse
   <int> <int>     <dbl>
 1     2    51     0.132
 2    12    67     0.134
 3     5    81     0.134
 4    15    34     0.134
 5     9    22     0.135
 6    22    42     0.136
 7    18    82     0.136
 8     8   121     0.137
 9    19   108     0.138
10    33    46     0.138

What’s notable?

  • After cross validation, the best RMSE is 0.132, with mtry = 51 and min_n = 2.
  • This is not better than glmnet. Also, cross validation of ranger takes much longer: about 164 seconds, against 11 seconds for glmnet.

Here is a plot of the ranger hyperparameter grid, with the best combination:

eda_plot_scatter(param_grid_rf, "min_n", "mtry", alpha = 1, add_lm = F) +
  geom_point(data = param_best_rf, aes(x = min_n, y = mtry), color = "red") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = param_best_rf, aes(x = min_n, y = mtry, label = glue::glue("mtry: {mtry}, min_n:{min_n}")), family = "Roboto Condensed")

xgboost

xgboost (gradient boosting) builds decision trees one after the other. Each new tree corrects some of the errors of the trees before it. Each model has 1000 trees, and we search for the best values of these hyperparameters:

  • min_n: the minimum number of properties that a group (node) must have before the tree can split it again.
  • tree_depth: the maximum number of questions (splits) from the top of a tree to its bottom.
  • learn_rate: how much each new tree can change the predictions. A smaller value makes the model learn more slowly and carefully.
model_spec_xgboost
Boosted Tree Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  trees = 1000
  min_n = tune()
  tree_depth = tune()
  learn_rate = tune()

Engine-Specific Arguments:
  objective = reg:squarederror
  nthread = 1

Computational engine: xgboost

Here are the 10 best RMSE values and their hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_xgboost %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 4
   min_n tree_depth learn_rate mean_rmse
   <int>      <int>      <dbl>     <dbl>
 1    33          2    0.0289      0.125
 2     3          2    0.0171      0.127
 3    23          4    0.0254      0.128
 4    24          1    0.190       0.129
 5    11          5    0.0549      0.129
 6    32          9    0.00605     0.130
 7    19         11    0.00482     0.130
 8    16         14    0.0121      0.131
 9    38          9    0.0270      0.131
10    23          9    0.0405      0.131

What’s notable?

  • After cross validation, the best RMSE is 0.125, with min_n = 33, tree_depth = 2 and learn_rate = 0.0289.
  • This is the best cross validated RMSE of all the models. It is a little better than glmnet (0.129) and ranger (0.132).
  • Cross validation of xgboost takes longer than glmnet, but it is faster than ranger (about 137 seconds).

Finalizing Models

For each model, we now know the hyperparameters with the lowest RMSE. We use them to train each model again on the complete training set. Then we use the trained models to predict log(SalePrice) for the training set, and we compare the predictions with the actual values.

# Get predicted estimates
get_predicted <- function(model_final, dfNew) {

  # Predict on testing set
  vEstimates <- model_final %>%
    predict(new_data = dfNew) %>%
    pull(.pred)
  
  return(vEstimates)
}

dfResults_train <- dfTrain %>% 
  mutate(actual = log(SalePrice)) %>% 
  select(Id, actual) %>% 
  mutate(glmnet = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_glmnet, dfTrain_Proc),
         ranger = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_rf, dfTrain_Proc),
         xgboost = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_xgboost, dfTrain_Proc))
dfPlot <- dfResults_train %>% 
  gather(model, predicted, -actual, -Id) %>% 
  mutate(model = ordered(model, levels = c("glmnet","ranger","xgboost")))

dfPlot %>%
  rename(`log(SalePrice)` = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("log(SalePrice)", "predicted", feature_model = "model", feature_id = "Id", nLabel = 3) +
  labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted log(SalePrice) on training set")

# properties among the 3 largest errors of more than one model
dfWorst_train <- dfPlot %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  slice_max(abs(predicted - actual), n = 3) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  count(Id, name = "n_models") %>%
  filter(n_models > 1) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_models))

# sentence about the properties that are among the largest errors of the most models
worst_train_sentence <- if (nrow(dfWorst_train) == 0) {
  "No property is among them for more than one model."
} else {
  vIds <- dfWorst_train$Id[dfWorst_train$n_models == max(dfWorst_train$n_models)]
  glue::glue("{if (length(vIds) == 1) 'The property with Id' else 'The properties with Ids'} {paste0('__', vIds, '__', collapse = ' and ')} {if (length(vIds) == 1) 'is' else 'are each'} among them for {max(dfWorst_train$n_models)} of the 3 models, so we should check {if (length(vIds) == 1) 'its' else 'their'} data for errors.")
}

What’s notable?

  • ranger and xgboost fit the training data closely: their predictions are near the 45-degree line, where the predicted value is equal to the actual value. ranger fits the training data most closely, with a training RMSE of 0.050, against 0.096 for xgboost.
  • The glmnet model has two outliers, Ids 524 and 1299. Their predicted prices are much higher than their actual prices. Also, for the cheaper properties, the predicted values are very spread out.
  • The plots label the three largest errors of each model. The properties with Ids 31 and 1299 are each among them for 2 of the 3 models, so we should check their data for errors.
  • But a good fit on the training data does not prove that a model is good. We can only measure its true performance on data that it has not seen: the testing set.

Performance on Test Data

dfResults_test <- dfTest %>% 
  mutate(actual = log(SalePrice)) %>% 
  select(Id, actual) %>% 
  mutate(glmnet = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_glmnet, dfTest_Proc),
         ranger = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_rf, dfTest_Proc),
         xgboost = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_xgboost, dfTest_Proc))
dfPlot <- dfResults_test %>% 
  gather(model, predicted, -actual, -Id) %>% 
  mutate(model = ordered(model, levels = c("glmnet","ranger","xgboost")))

dfPlot %>%
  rename(`log(SalePrice)` = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("log(SalePrice)", "predicted", feature_model = "model", feature_id = "Id", nLabel = 3) +
  labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted log(SalePrice) on testing set")

dfRMSE <- map(list("glmnet","ranger","xgboost"), ~ rmse(dfResults_test, actual, !!sym(.x)) %>% mutate(model = .x)) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(cv_rmse = c(cv_results_glmnet$mean_rmse[1], cv_results_rf$mean_rmse[1], cv_results_xgboost$mean_rmse[1])) %>%
  select(-.estimator, -.metric) %>%
  rename(test_rmse = .estimate) %>%
  select(model, everything())

dfRMSE
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  model   test_rmse cv_rmse
  <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl>
1 glmnet      0.130   0.129
2 ranger      0.138   0.132
3 xgboost     0.132   0.125

What’s notable?

  • For all the models, the RMSE on the testing set is similar to the cross validated RMSE. This shows that cross validation correctly estimated how well the models work on new data, and that the hyperparameters are good.
  • The properties with Ids 1537 and 2217 are outliers: no model predicts a price close to their actual prices.
  • glmnet has the lowest RMSE on the testing set, 0.130. xgboost is close, with 0.132.
  • But outliers affect glmnet, as we saw with Ids 524 and 1299 in the training set. xgboost had the best cross validated RMSE, and the difference on the testing set is small. Also, xgboost is less affected by outliers, and it can learn curved relationships. So we choose xgboost as our final model, because it works well on new data.
model_final <- model_final_xgboost

Feature Importance

It is harder to understand how xgboost makes its predictions than how a linear model makes them. But a variable importance plot can show which features are the most important for the model.

Here are the 10 most important features of our final xgboost model:

library(vip)

p1 <- vip(extract_fit_parsnip(model_final), aesthetics = list(fill = "#00AED8")) +
  labs(title = "xgboost model Feature Importance in Training") +
  theme_quant()

vFeaturesImp <- vip::vi(extract_fit_parsnip(model_final)) %>% top_n(10, Importance) %>% pull(Variable)

p2 <- eda_plot_correlation_matrix(dfTrain %>% select(SalePrice, one_of(vFeaturesImp)), 
                            outlineVar = "SalePrice", plotTitle = "Correlations with SalePrice")

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), nrow = 1)

  • The plot on the right shows the correlations of the numerical features. All of them have a correlation of at least 0.5, or at most -0.5, with SalePrice.
  • All of the 10 most important features make sense. To judge the price of a property, a buyer would look at the total area, the overall quality, the neighborhood, the number of bathrooms, the kitchen quality, the age of the property, the size and finish of the garage, central air conditioning, the overall condition, and so on.
  • So our final model works well on new data, and it chooses very reasonable features.

New Property Premium

Of the 10 most important features in our final model, most do not change during the life of a property, such as the area, the neighborhood and the number of bathrooms. The quality and the condition of a property can change, but people judge them in different ways. The only feature that clearly changes over time is PropertyAge.

So, how does the predicted SalePrice change with the age of a property? We compare the same property when it is new, when it is more than 30 years old, and at all the ages in between.

We choose two properties at random, change their PropertyAge, and look at the effect on the predicted SalePrice.

getSampleProperty <- function(randomSeed) {
  
  set.seed(randomSeed)
  dfSample <- dfTest %>% 
    filter(PropertyAge >= 30) %>% 
    sample_n(1)
  
  dfSample <- tibble(PropertyAge = 1:dfSample$PropertyAge[1]) %>% expand_grid(dfSample %>% select(-PropertyAge))
}

dfSample <- getSampleProperty(1000) %>% bind_rows(getSampleProperty(2000))

# preprocess the sample data with the recipe prepared on the training set and generate predicted values from the final model
bake(preprocessing_recipe, new_data = dfSample) %>% 
  get_predicted(model_final, .) %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  bind_cols(dfSample) %>% 
  mutate(predicted = exp(value)) %>% 
  group_by(Id) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PropertyAge, y = predicted)) +
  geom_point(color = "#00AED8") +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~Id, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(y = "Predicted Sale Price",
       title = "New Property Premium")

A new property sells for a little more than an older property of the same type, quality and condition. This premium is small in a place like Ames, Iowa. We expect it to be much higher in a large city.

item.title: Diamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear Models
item.description:
In a previous post in this series, we explored the diamonds dataset. We found that price has a strong correlation with carat, x, y and z, and that log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat). For diamonds of similar weight, clarity and color also seemed to help predict the price.

In this post, we build linear models and find out how well they predict the price of diamonds. A linear model predicts a value by adding up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that the model learns from the data.

First, let’s build a simple base model that uses all the features, without any changes to them. Its results give us a starting point to compare with:

model_lm <- lm(price ~ ., data = diamonds)
summary(model_lm)

2 rsq     standard       0.920
3 mae     standard     740.

The model summary shows that this model is overfitted. An overfitted model learns the noise in the data, not only the true patterns, so it does not work well on new data. For example, we know that depth and table have no effect on price, but the model says that they are very important.

The table above also shows the root mean squared error (RMSE) and other metrics. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, in the same units as the price. A lower RMSE means better predictions.

Let’s plot the actual prices against the predicted prices, to see how well this base model works.

augment(model_lm, diamonds) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", ".fitted", nLabel = 0, labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted price from a base linear model")

If the predictions are good, the points are close to the dashed line at 45 degrees, where the predicted price is equal to the actual price. This base model predicts the prices badly. Worst of all, it predicts negative prices for cheap diamonds. To prevent such impossible results, we must use log(price) instead of price.

Feature Engineering

Feature engineering means that we create new features from the existing features, to make the patterns easier for a model to learn.

We know that the price of a diamond has a strong correlation with its size. If all other things are equal, a larger diamond has a higher price.

As a first estimate, we can treat a diamond as a box with the dimensions x, y and z. Then its volume is x * y * z. These 3 dimensions have a strong correlation with each other. So we can calculate one average dimension as the cube root of volume. This average dimension keeps a straight-line relationship with log(price).

We can also calculate an average dimension with high school chemistry. Mass, volume and density are related by this equation:

$ density = mass/volume $

1 carat is 0.2 grams. If we divide the mass by the density of diamond (3.51 grams per cubic centimeter), we get the volume. The cube root of the volume gives an average dimension.

dfInput <- diamonds %>%
  mutate(row = row_number(),
         volume = x*y*z,
         `average dimension` = volume ^ (1/3),
         volume2 = carat * 0.2/3.51,
         `average dimension2` = (volume2 ^ (1/3)) * 10)   # Multiply by 10 to convert from cm to mm

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, c("average dimension", "average dimension2"), "price", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar,
                 nLabel = 3, feature_id = "row", labelBy = "leverage") +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of price v/s average dimension")

# the point with the most leverage on the linear fit of price on the dimension-based feature
dfLeverage <- dfInput %>%
  mutate(leverage = hatvalues(lm(price ~ `average dimension`, data = dfInput))) %>%
  slice_max(leverage, n = 1)

The two methods give similar results, but the density method gives a narrower range. Which method is more reliable? In each panel, the labels show the row numbers of the diamonds with the most leverage. Leverage tells how much a point can pull the straight line towards itself. Points that are far from the others along the x axis have the most leverage. With the dimensions, the most extreme point is the diamond in row 24068. It is a 2 carat diamond with a recorded width y of 58.9 mm. This value is clearly a recording error. The other labelled points are diamonds with an average dimension of 0. With the density method, the labelled points are simply the largest diamonds in the dataset. Also, 20 values of z are 0. In 7 of these diamonds, x and y are also 0. So these dimensions were not recorded correctly.

For all of these diamonds, the carat values are correct. So carat is probably more accurate than the dimensions, and we prefer the density method to create this feature.

Also, the density is a constant. So we do not need to divide by it to calculate the volume. Instead, we can take the cube root of carat itself. Then we expect a straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(carat^{1/3}\). A straight-line relationship is what a linear model needs, because the model adds up its features in a straight-line way.

The geometry suggests a cube root. But does the cube root give the best straight line? Let’s compare it with other transforms. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points of log(price):

p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(diamonds, "carat", "price")
p_transforms

vR2_carat <- p_transforms$data %>%
  distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
  pull(r_squared) %>%
  set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))

The cube root (R-squared 0.924) is much better than carat without a transform (0.847). But log(carat) is even better (0.933). A straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(log(carat)\) is easy to understand: the coefficient of \(log(carat)\) is the percentage change in price when carat increases by 1%. We will try both transforms in our models.

Training Linear Models

These are the steps to build the linear models and measure how well they work:

  • Split the dataset into two sets: a training set with 75% of the diamonds and a testing set with 25%. The model learns from the training set. Then we check its predictions on the testing set, which has diamonds that the model has not seen.
  • clarity is one of the most important features. So we split the data in a way that keeps the same mix of clarity grades in both sets. This is called stratified sampling.
  • Train (fit) a linear model on the training set.
  • Make predictions on the testing set and calculate the metrics.
  • Put all the steps above in a function that takes the model formula and a random seed. The seed controls which diamonds go into each set. With different seeds, we get different random splits, so one lucky or unlucky split does not decide the results.
  • Run each model several times with different seeds, and calculate its average metrics. These averages show how well the model works on new data.

Here is one split into a training set and a testing set, stratified by clarity. Both sets have a similar mix of clarity grades.

set.seed(1333)
train_split <- diamonds %>% 
  select(price, everything()) %>% 
  initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")

dfTrain <- training(train_split)
dfTest <- testing(train_split)

We ran each model 5 times with different seeds. Here are the average metrics. R-squared (rsq) tells how much of the variation in price the model explains, and the mean absolute error (mae) is the average size of a prediction error:

fit_linear_model <- function(randomSeed, model_formula, get_model = FALSE) {

  set.seed(randomSeed)
  train_split <- diamonds %>% 
    select(price, everything()) %>% 
    initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")
  
  dfTrain <- training(train_split)
  dfTest <- testing(train_split)

  # fit a linear model
  model_lm <- lm(model_formula, data = dfTrain)
  
  # predict on testing set to determine rmse  
  predict_lm <- predict(model_lm, dfTest)

  # predict on testing set with outliers
  dfResults <- dfTest %>% 
    mutate(actual = price) %>% 
    mutate(estimate = predict_lm %>% exp()) %>% 
    select(actual, estimate)
  
  if(get_model) {
    return(list(model_lm, dfResults))
  } else {
    return(dfResults)
  }
}
set.seed(1000)
vRandomSeeds <- sample(9999, 5)
dfModels <- expand_grid(seed = vRandomSeeds, 
                        model = c("log(price) ~ .",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3))",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color + cut",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat)",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color + cut")) %>%
  mutate(results = map2(seed, model, ~ fit_linear_model(.x, as.formula(.y)))) %>% 
  mutate(metrics = map(results, ~ metrics(.x, truth = actual, estimate = estimate))) %>%
  select(-results) %>% 
  unnest(cols = metrics) %>% 
  select(-.estimator) %>% 
  spread(.metric, .estimate) %>% 
  group_by(model) %>% 
  summarise_at(vars(rmse, rsq, mae), mean)

The first model, with all the features, is overfitted.

Each model with log(carat) is much better than the same model with the cube root of carat. With clarity and color, the RMSE goes down from $1,725 to $816, and the R-squared goes up from 0.888 to 0.959.

The model with log(carat), clarity and color gives the best combination of a low RMSE and a high R-squared, so it explains the most variation. This is our final model. If we add cut, the RMSE goes down only a little, to $795. So we do not use cut, and we keep the model simpler.

A residual is the difference between the actual value and the predicted value, here of log(price). Residual plots show if the errors of a model have a pattern. If the model is good, the residuals look like random noise around 0. Here are the four standard residual plots of our final model:

# labels are off: the row numbers of a random training set do not identify the diamonds
eda_plot_residuals(fit_lm[[1]], nLabel = 0)

vStdResid <- rstandard(fit_lm[[1]])
vCooks <- cooks.distance(fit_lm[[1]])
  • Residuals vs Fitted: The residuals stay close to 0 for all predicted values, and the red smooth line is almost flat. So the model captures the relationship well. The small curve shows that a little non-linearity remains. At the highest predicted values, the residuals form a sloping edge below 0. The reason is that no diamond in the data costs more than $18,823, so for the largest predictions, the actual price can only be lower.
  • Normal Q-Q: In the middle, the points follow the dashed line, so most residuals are normally distributed. But the tails, especially the upper tail, are longer: some diamonds cost much more than the model predicts. 160 of the 40453 diamonds in the training set have a standardized residual larger than 3, or smaller than -3.
  • Scale-Location: The smooth line is almost flat, so the spread of the errors is about the same for cheap and expensive diamonds. The log of price makes the spread stable. Without it, the errors grow with the price.
  • Residuals vs Leverage: No diamond has a high leverage. The largest Cook’s distance is only 0.0067. A point needs a Cook’s distance of about 0.5 or more to pull the model strongly, so the plot does not even reach the dashed contours that mark 0.5 and 1. No single diamond controls the model.

If clarity and color do not change, a 1% increase in carat increases the predicted price by about 1.88%.

Here is a scatter plot of the actual prices against the prices that our final model predicts for the testing set:

fit_lm[[2]] %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", nLabel = 0, xLog = T, yLog = T,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = bquote(log(price) == log(carat) + clarity + color))

The points are close to the 45-degree line. But at the high end, the differences between the actual and predicted prices become larger. The predictions of the final model are also much less extreme. The most expensive diamond in the testing set costs $18,804. The highest predicted price is $28,130. But the cube root model predicts prices as high as $59,082 for the same testing set. Like all linear models, the final model can still predict prices above the highest prices in the data (this is called extrapolation).
